New to Irish Dancing? Start Here 🌸
A plain-language guide for dancers, parents & newcomers to the feis world
💃
What is a Feis?
A feis (pronounced "fesh", plural: feiseanna) is an Irish dancing competition — usually held on weekends in community halls or hotels. Dancers compete in age groups and levels, from beginner (Primary) through to the most advanced (Prizewinner / Open Championship). Medals, trophies, and recall points are awarded. Think of it as a gymnastics meet, but for feet! 🏆
🥇
Levels Explained
Dancers advance through levels by winning or placing well at feiseanna. The typical progression is: Primary → Beginner → Advanced Beginner → Novice → Prizewinner → Preliminary Champion → Open Champion. At the top sits the World Championship (An Chomhdhail) — the biggest event in Irish dance, held every year at Easter. Getting there takes years of dedication! 🌟
👟
Soft Shoes vs Hard Shoes
Soft shoes (pumps / ghillies) look like ballet slippers and are worn for reels, light jigs, and slip jigs. They create graceful, flowing movement. Hard shoes (heavies / jig shoes) have a fiberglass tip and heel that make rhythmic clicking sounds — worn for hornpipes, treble jigs, and set dances. Many dancers train both styles from the start. 👠
🎗️
Dress & Appearance
Competition dresses are elaborate, embroidered, and often custom-made. Colours and emblem designs are unique to each dance school (feachool). Hair is worn in curls — either a wig or natural curls in a bun. At lower levels, simpler dresses are fine, but as dancers advance, competition-specific dresses become more important. Solo dresses can cost anywhere from €200 to €2,000+. 💎
📅
What is the Oireachtas?
The Oireachtas (pronounced "oh-RECK-tus") is a major regional championship — one step below the World Championships. Qualifying at the Oireachtas earns a dancer the right to compete at Worlds. In Ireland, the All-Ireland Oireachtas is held in November. It is hugely prestigious — getting on stage there is a huge achievement for any dancer. 🌍
💪
Why Train Off-Stage?
Irish dancing is incredibly physically demanding — it requires explosive power, balance, core stability, hip mobility, and cardiovascular endurance. Most injuries happen because certain muscles are over-trained while others are neglected. This app helps dancers and parents build a balanced training plan that supports class work and reduces injury risk — especially important as competitions get more intense. 🧠
🔵
Understanding the Colour Dots
Throughout this app, exercises are labelled with a small coloured dot. A gold dot means Compound — the exercise trains 4 or more muscle groups at once and gives you the most return per minute of training. A pink dot means Focused — it targets one or two specific muscles and is best used when you know you have a particular weak spot. Beginners: start with compound exercises! ✨
🧘
How to Use This App
Start with Feis Goals — pick the movement quality you most want to improve (e.g. "higher kicks" or "better turnout"). The app shows you exactly which muscles are involved, which exercises target them, and the science behind it. Then visit Build a Session to tick exercises and create a printable training plan. Not sure where to start? Talk to your dance teacher about what the judge feedback says! 💬

Injury Prevention 🩹
Based on peer-reviewed research — Journal of Dance Medicine & Science, PMC systematic review of Irish dancing injuries
📊 What the research shows: A 2023 systematic review of Irish dance injuries found stress fractures are the most prevalent diagnosis (29.9% of clinical cases), followed by patellofemoral pain syndrome (11.1%), ankle sprains (5.1%), and plantar fasciitis (4.6%). 79.6% of injuries are overuse in nature — meaning they are largely preventable with smart training. 58% of injuries occur before major competitions, exactly when training load is highest.
